did_you_know.text: The war between the house of Saul and the house of David lasted a long time, but the trend was the opposite: David grew stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker.
David’s sons were born in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, the son of Ahinoam of Jezreel.
Absalom, David’s third son, was the son of Maakah, the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. This detail indicates a family connection between David’s house and a foreign kingdom.
During the war, Abner was the powerful leader of Saul’s house, rather than Ish-bosheth, who was the official king.
The conflict between Ish-bosheth and Abner concerned Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine. Abner viewed Ish-bosheth’s words as a serious accusation against his honor and loyalty.
Abner declared that he intended to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and establish David’s throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.
David agreed to make a covenant with Abner, but first demanded the return of Saul’s daughter Michal, who had been his wife and had meanwhile married Palti son of Laish.
Abner spoke with the elders of Israel and with the people of Benjamin to advance David’s kingship. The Benjamites were Saul’s tribe.
Joab killed Abner in Hebron to avenge the death of his brother Asahel, even though he did so without David’s knowledge and contrary to the agreement made with Abner.
After Abner was buried, the people and all Israel understood that David had not ordered his death, partly because of the public mourning, lament, and fast that David observed.
